A_target.statement:
Let $L \subseteq \Sigma^*$.
Then $L$ is [[Definition:Regular Language|regular]] {{iff}} there exist a [[Definition:Finite Monoid|finite monoid]] $M$, a [[Definition:Monoid Homomorphism|monoid homomorphism]] $h: \Sigma^* \to M$ and $F \subseteq M$ with:
:$L = \map {h^{-1} } F$

B_source.statement: [[Definition:Finite Monoid|Finite monoids]] are closed under [[Definition:Direct Product|direct products]], [[Definition:Submonoid|submonoids]] and [[Definition:Quotient Monoid|quotients]].

substitutions.the finite monoid: the transition monoid of an automaton, or the syntactic monoid of the language
substitutions.a monoid homomorphism: the map sending a word to the transformation it induces

derived.closure under Boolean operations: the same monoid recognizes the complement and, via products, intersections
derived.the minimal recognizing monoid: the syntactic monoid, the analogue of the minimal automaton

object_map.reformulation: Regard words as elements of a free monoid, so that recognition becomes a homomorphism into a finite monoid.

validity_conditions: Concatenation of words is associative with the empty word as identity, so words form a free monoid and a language is a subset of it.
Recognition by a finite monoid is equivalent to recognition by a finite automaton, since the transition monoid is finite and conversely a monoid yields an automaton.
Properties not expressible in monoid terms do not transfer; the correspondence is with regular languages only, so context-free phenomena fall outside it entirely.
proof_plan: Regard $\Sigma^*$ as the [[Definition:Free Monoid|free monoid]] on $\Sigma$ under concatenation.

Given a [[Definition:Deterministic Finite Automaton|DFA]] with state set $Q$, map each word $w$ to the transformation $\delta_w: Q \to Q$ it induces.
The set of such transformations is a finite monoid, the [[Definition:Transition Monoid|transition monoid]], and $w \mapsto \delta_w$ is a homomorphism.

Let $F = \set {\delta: \map \delta {q_0} \in Q_F}$.
Then $L = \map {h^{-1} } F$.
Conversely, $M$ itself acts as the state set of a DFA recognizing $\map {h^{-1} } F$.

If $L_i = \map {h_i^{-1} } {F_i}$ for $i = 1, 2$, then $L_1 \cap L_2$ is recognized by $M_1 \times M_2$.
Complement is recognized by $M \setminus F$.
Hence closure properties follow from monoid constructions.
{{qed}}
